Questions are the head-term queries the homepage owns per the IA plan's intent-ownership matrix; the deeper 'which limit for which food' questions belong on the regulation and product pages that own them. Answers are hand-authored prose — {{placeholders}} are filled with live counts by tools/build-homepage.mjs, so no number is typed here. Every question and answer is run through tools/lib/faq-firewall-guard.mjs at build time and again at JSON-LD time; an item that trips the firewall is dropped, never softened.

items.q: Which heavy metals turn up in food?
items.a: The ones that recur across the food supply are lead, cadmium, arsenic and mercury, with nickel, aluminium, chromium and tin appearing in narrower sets of products. Arsenic and mercury are tracked as species rather than totals, because inorganic arsenic and methylmercury are the forms that drive toxicity and the forms most regulatory limits are written against. The Index carries {{metal_pages}} metal pages, each covering the toxicology, the exposure routes and the limits that apply.

items.q: How do heavy metals get into food in the first place?
items.a: Mostly through the environment rather than through manufacturing. Lead and cadmium sit in soil from historical leaded fuel, paint and industrial emissions and are taken up by crops. Arsenic is drawn from groundwater and soil by rice, which floods during growing. Mercury accumulates up the marine food chain, so the largest predatory fish carry the most. Nickel and chromium can be picked up from processing equipment, and packaging contributes in specific categories. Because the pathways are environmental, contamination tends to track the commodity and where it was grown before it tracks any particular producer.

items.q: Is there a safe level of lead in food?
items.a: No major regulatory body has identified a blood lead level in children below which harm is not observed. EFSA withdrew the tolerable weekly intake for lead in 2010 on the basis that no health-protective value could be derived, JECFA withdrew its own the same year, and the US EPA does not derive an oral reference dose. The operative framing across agencies is to reduce exposure as far as practicable rather than to stay under a single number. See the lead page for the full regulatory position and the studies behind it.

items.q: Which foods carry the most heavy metals?
items.a: It depends on the metal. Rice and rice-derived ingredients dominate inorganic arsenic; large predatory fish dominate methylmercury; cocoa, leafy greens and some root vegetables carry the most cadmium; spices and some botanicals are recurring lead findings. The Index reports these at the ingredient level, where the contamination originates, and again at the product-category level, where a consumer encounters it — {{ingredient_pages}} ingredient profiles and {{product_pages}} product categories.

items.q: Who sets the limits for heavy metals in food?
items.a: Different bodies set different kinds of value, and they are not interchangeable. Codex Alimentarius publishes international maximum levels; the European Commission sets binding maximum levels for the EU; the US FDA issues action levels and guidance rather than binding limits for most foods; EFSA and JECFA derive health-based intake values that inform the others but are not themselves limits; and state programmes such as California's Proposition 65 set their own thresholds. The Index carries {{regulation_pages}} regulation pages, each stating the exact value, the matrix it applies to and the basis it is measured on.

items.q: Does the Index test products or rank brands?
items.a: No. The Index reports what the published literature and regulatory record say about metals, ingredients and product categories. It does not test products, does not name brands in its findings, and does not publish brand-by-brand tables. Where third-party testing is cited as a source, the category-level and ingredient-level signal is summarised and the reader is pointed at the original for anything brand-specific.

items.q: How complete is the evidence behind these pages?
items.a: Partially, and the Index says so on the record. The coverage page reports how many papers the literature search identified against how many have been promoted to source pages, broken out by category, so a reader can see where the corpus is deep and where it is thin. {{source_pages}} source pages are indexed so far. Pages whose evidence is sparse carry a low confidence marker rather than a confident-looking number.

items.q: Can I check a claim on any page back to its source?
items.a: Yes, and that is the point of the structure. Every figure links to a source record carrying the study's citation, its methods, the values extracted from it and the file hash of the document those values were read out of. Each page also lists its references in citation order, alongside the wider set of sources routed to it, and records its own edit history so a page can be reconstructed as it stood on a given date.
